name: Spanish Green
lede: Spanish green is an old name for verdigris, the copper green painters relied on for centuries; the bright green swatch on screens today has little in common with it.

sections.title: Verdigris by another name
sections.body:
In English, verdigris takes its name from a French phrase meaning "green of Greece", while the Germans call it *Grünspan*, "Spanish green" [1][2]. The Pigment Compendium says the German word is believed to come from the Latin *viride hispanicum* [3]. Finlay suggests the pigment probably reached both places through the Arabs [2], and the scholar Agricola, in the 1500s, gave Spain as its source [4].

The Compendium cites Theophilus, writing around the twelfth century, who describes two preparations: *viride salsum* and *viride hispanicum*, the latter made by exposing copper to vinegar or urine [3]. Many writers did not distinguish the preparations [3]. A later study found that old recipes produced mixtures of copper salts, with copper acetates and some malachite and atacamite [3].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
Until the 1800s no green on a painter's palette was livelier than verdigris, yet it was unstable, and it blackens or browns beside ultramarine, orpiment and other pigments that contain sulphur [5]. In the 1670s the Dutch painter Samuel van Hoogstraten complained that green earth was too weak, Spanish green too crude, and verditer not durable enough [6][4]. Ball reports that Velázquez never used a pure green pigment, mixing his greens instead [6].

The swatch here is not that pigment. It is a vivid, clean [[green]] that Maerz and Paul record as first used around 1450, and the ISCC-NBS system lists it as a block of its own [7]. Its nearest named neighbor is [[sea-green]], and it sits among greens such as [[emerald-green]] and [[hunter-green]] [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This green is rare in paintings: 3 of 23,781 in our archive, rarer than 77 per cent of named colors, led by Edvard Munch around 1903 [8]. Verdigris itself darkens and browns with age, so it would not match this swatch in old paintings. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test. [8]

origin.named_after: the German name Grünspan for verdigris, from viride hispanicum
